Out of {{< var current_disease_patients_global >}} with chronic disease, only {{< var current_trial_slots_available >}} participate in trials annually [@global-trial-participant-capacity]. That's **{{< var current_clinical_trial_participation_rate >}}**.

Half of humanity would volunteer [@patient-willingness-clinical-trials] if they could. We have **240 times more willing participants** than we're using.

This isn't because people don't want to help find cures. It's because the current system can't scale. Trials cost {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}, require traveling to major medical centers, and have exclusion criteria that reject {{< var antidepressant_trial_exclusion_rate >}} of actual patients [@antidepressant-trial-exclusion-rates].

**We're not facing a recruitment problem. We're facing a capacity problem.**

## The Solution: Consumer Reports for Drugs

Your decentralized framework for drug assessment (dFDA) is an **open coordination protocol** that enables existing platforms to connect companies with treatments to patients who need them. It's HTTP for clinical trials - a standard that lets all the existing systems talk to each other and share outcomes.

![The FDA, but run by software. All the same boxes, fewer humans to corrupt.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-the-solution-consumer-reports-for-drugs-bw-academic.jpg)

### How Companies Register Treatments (5 Minutes, Zero Approval Needed)

**Any company** - pharma, supplements, food, interventions - can instantly create a trial:

1. **Register treatment** on a public portal (name, ingredients, condition, price)
2. **Set treatment price** (what you charge patients - covers manufacturing + delivery)
3. **Get automatic liability insurance** (built into protocol governance)
4. **Trial goes live immediately** - appears in search results, ranked by existing data
5. **Patients join** based on rankings → You collect zero-cost data on whether it works

#### Net cost to company: $0

![Patients pay for their own medicine, then you give them their money back, and somehow everyone profits. Economics is confusing.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-net-cost-to-company-0-bw-academic.jpg)

**Why?**

- Patients pay for treatment (covers manufacturing/delivery)
- Patients provide data (eliminates data collection cost ~{{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}/patient)
- Protocol enables standardized analysis (eliminates analysis cost)
- Insurance is built-in (eliminates liability cost)

### The Payment Flow (Or: How Everyone Profits Except Disease)

![Money goes from patient to fund to patient to company to fund to patient. It's a circle, like water cycle but for dollars.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-the-payment-flow-or-how-everyone-profits-except-disease-bw-academic.jpg)

**Patient pays:** Treatment cost + Refundable deposit
**Patient receives:** Subsidy (from a 1% Treaty Fund)
**Patient reports:** Outcomes via simple app
**Deposit refunded:** When trial complete
**Net to patient:** $0 to -$50 (they might profit)

#### Example

- Patient joins trial for experimental migraine treatment ($100/month)
- Pays: $100 treatment + $50 deposit = $150
- Receives: $125 subsidy
- Out of pocket: $25
- Completes trial, reports outcomes
- Gets back: $50 deposit
- **Net: +$25 profit + potentially cures migraines**

![Everyone gets paid, patient pays nothing. If this sounds impossible, you're thinking like an economist instead of a magician.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-economic-flow-diagram-bw-academic.jpg)

#### Company receives

![Companies make a little money from selling pills and a lot of money from knowing which pills work. Information is expensive, apparently.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-company-receives-bw-academic.jpg)

- $100/month from patient
- Manufacturing cost: $20/month
- Profit: $80/month per patient
- Plus: Free clinical trial data worth {{< var traditional_phase3_cost_per_patient >}}/patient in traditional system

### Why This Creates Unlimited Research Capacity

#### Traditional model (bottleneck)
```
Research ideas → Grant committees → Selected few → $57M per trial → ~10 trials/year per company
```

**Decentralized protocol (unlimited):**
```
Research ideas → Register instantly → Patients decide by joining → $0 per trial → Unlimited trials simultaneously
```

**This is why 95% of rare diseases have no treatments.** Traditional funding can't afford to test everything. This decentralized protocol enables testing EVERYTHING because:

- No approval bottleneck (instant registration)
- No funding bottleneck (patients pay for treatment)
- No data collection bottleneck (patients provide data)
- No disease too rare (if 100 patients exist globally, trial can run profitably)

**Traditional trial:** Pharma spends $57M, tests most profitable drug only
**Decentralized trial:** Pharma spends $0, tests everything including supplements, food, lifestyle, off-patent drugs

A 1% Treaty Fund doesn't fund pragmatic clinical trials directly. **It subsidizes participation, which unlocks a self-sustaining ecosystem that funds ALL research.**

![One research lab doing one thing at a time versus a million people doing a million things at once. Speed difference is noticeable.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-bottleneck-vs-protocol-process-bw-academic.jpg)

## How It Works: Just Let People Try Stuff (Carefully)

Here's a thought that apparently never occurred to anyone in Washington:

What if sick people could just... try treatments?

And then we could... write down what happens?

And then other sick people could... see what worked?

Your current system leaves 95% of rare diseases [@95-pct-diseases-no-treatment] with zero approved treatments and ensures 85% of patients are barred [@fda-trial-patient-exclusion-criteria] from the trials that might save them. We've managed to perfect a system where only the healthy and compliant are allowed to test cures for the sick and desperate. It's genius, in a suicidal sort of way.

This is because trials are designed to test drugs on people who don't actually exist. To get into a study for an antidepressant, for example, you can't have any other pesky problems like anxiety or PTSD. You can't have a history of drug or alcohol use. You can't be on other medications. You have to be the *perfect* kind of sick. The result? One investigation found that only 14.5% [@pubmed-14628985] of real-world patients with depression would actually qualify. The rest of us are too messy for their pristine, clean data.

On top of excluding everyone with a pulse, these "definitive" studies are run on comically small groups. They'll test a new heart drug on 275 people [@us-trial-enrollment-targets-2009], a cancer drug on just 20 people [@us-trial-enrollment-targets-2009], and a diabetes drug on 100 people [@us-trial-enrollment-targets-2009], then prescribe the winner to millions.

![We tested this drug on thirty-six people and then gave it to millions. Like taste-testing a pie with one person and serving it to a stadium.](../../assets/images/wellbutrin-effectiveness-small-sample-size.png)

We're basing the survival of our species on a sample size smaller than a kindergarten class. So, instead of studying these mythical, perfectly sick unicorns, what if we just collected data from everyone who's *actually* sick?

### The Power of Real-World Evidence (Or: Spying on Sick People for a Good Cause)

This framework is built on a simple, powerful, and slightly creepy idea: we can learn more, faster, by analyzing data from real patients in the real world. This is called Real-World Evidence (RWE), which is a fancy term for "watching what happens."

Skeptics will say, "But that's just observational research! Correlation isn't causation!" They'll point to flip-flopping diet advice about eggs and cholesterol as proof that this is all voodoo.

They're not wrong about the old way. Old observational studies were flawed because they couldn't easily separate correlation from causation. Did the people who ate eggs also smoke three packs a day? The studies couldn't always tell.

But here's what's changed: we now have so much data and such powerful computers that we can overcome these problems. With modern data from wearables, apps, and electronic health records, a single person can become their own control group. We can track someone's arthritis pain for a month, have them take Turmeric for a month, then stop, then start again. By doing this, we can see if the Turmeric is actually doing something or if it's just a coincidence.

Modern statistical methods are so good that a meta-analysis in the New England Journal of Medicine [@meta-analysis-in-the-new-england-journal-of-medicine] found that the results from high-quality observational studies are generally the same as those from expensive, slow randomized controlled trials.

![Watching what happens versus making it happen, and which one is better at predicting who dies.](../../assets/images/observational-vs-randomized-effect-sizes.png)

![Watching versus doing, and which one tells you the truth more often. Spoiler: they're surprisingly similar.](../../assets/images/observational-vs-randomized-trial-effect-sizes.png)

We have the tools to get reliable answers from real-world data. We just have to actually use them.

### Step 2.5: See the Future (With Financially-Backed Predictions)

To complement the real-world data from past patients, the system will integrate a powerful forecasting tool: **live prediction markets**.

![Lots of people guessing whether drugs will work, and the average of their guesses is usually right. The wisdom of crowds, betting edition.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-step-2-5-see-the-future-with-financially-backed-predictions-bw-academic.jpg)

This isn't just polling experts; it's a marketplace where researchers, doctors, investors, and even the public can bet real money on a trial's future outcomes.

For any given trial, you'll see real-time odds on questions like:

- **Effectiveness**: "What are the chances this treatment will reduce tumor size by >50% in the next 6 months?" **Market Price: 38%**
- **Adverse Events**: "What is the probability of patients experiencing severe nausea?" **Market Price: 22%**
- **Completion**: "What are the odds this trial will be fully enrolled by its target date?" **Market Price: 71%**

#### Why Trust This?

1.  **Skin in the Game**: These aren't cheap-talk opinions. Bettors lose money if they're wrong, creating a powerful incentive for accuracy.
2.  **The Ultimate Fact-Checker**: Your decentralized institutes of health (DIH) network automatically resolves these bets using the actual, aggregated, and anonymized patient data collected through the dFDA protocol. If the market predicts a 22% rate of nausea, and the real-world data shows 40%, the market learns and adjusts, or bettors go broke.

![People bet on drugs, patients take drugs, we check who won the bet. Like fantasy football but with your liver.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-why-trust-this-bw-academic.jpg)

This gives patients an invaluable second layer of information: not just what *has happened*, but what the world's collective, financially-incentivized intelligence thinks *will happen*.

## The Partnership Approach: Building Rails, Not Trains

Here's what we're NOT doing: building a government platform that competes with existing medical technology companies.

![One company owning the entire railway versus everyone sharing the tracks. We prefer sharing, as it's cheaper and less monopolistic.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-the-partnership-approach-building-rails-not-trains-bw-academic.jpg)

Here's what we ARE doing: establishing an open protocol that lets all the existing platforms talk to each other.

Think of it like the internet. We didn't build one website that everyone has to use. We built HTTP - the protocol that lets all websites connect. Same idea.

**How your framework gets funded:** An implementation of this framework is one of many campaigns competing for funding from the 1% Treaty Fund via [Wishocracy](wishocracy.qmd). It has no independent budget authority. If a particular implementation gets captured or fails to deliver, the community can fund alternative implementations instead. This prevents the "new FDA" problem.

### The Players Already in the Game

Multiple companies have already built decentralized clinical trial platforms, collectively raising hundreds of millions in venture funding [@dct-platform-funding-medable; @dct-platform-funding-others]. They're good at it. They have users. They have infrastructure.

Why compete with them? Partner instead.

**The protocol provides**:

- Open protocol for data exchange (like email protocols)
- Federated data network (data stays in Epic/Cerner/Apple Health systems)
- Treatment ranking algorithms (open source, anyone can verify)
- Trial matching services (connects patients to ANY platform)

**Existing platforms provide**:

- Patient-facing apps and interfaces
- Trial management tools
- Sponsor relationships
- Regional expertise

### Federated, Not Centralized

Data doesn't move to a central database. It stays where it is:

- Epic systems keep their data
- Apple Health keeps its data
- Cerner keeps its data

Your framework's protocol just lets you run queries ACROSS systems without moving data. Federated data networks already do this with 300M+ patient records.

![Instead of copying everyone's medical data to one place, we ask questions to many places and combine the answers. Your data stays where it is, we just visit.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-federated-not-centralized-bw-academic.jpg)

This solves:

- GDPR/HIPAA compliance (data never leaves source)
- Privacy concerns (no central honeypot to hack)
- Vendor cooperation (they keep control)
- Patient trust (data doesn't go to "the cloud")

## Why This Works: The Mathematical Impossibility of Committees

Here's the problem with having ~200 FDA bureaucrats [@fda-reviewer-count] decide what 8 billion people can try when they're dying:

### The Math That Proves Centralization Can't Work

Let's calculate how long it would take the FDA to properly evaluate every treatment for every person:

```{python}
# Information processing capacity of the FDA committee

committee_members = 200
hours_per_day = 8
decisions_per_hour = 1
committee_capacity = committee_members * hours_per_day * decisions_per_hour
# = 1,600 decisions/day

# Information that actually needs processing

![Multiply diseases by treatments by patients and you get 800 trillion possible medical decisions. That's more decisions than humans can make, which is problematic.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-information-that-actually-needs-processing-bw-academic.jpg)

diseases = 10_000
treatments_per_disease = 100  # Potential treatments to evaluate
patients = 8_000_000_000
patient_variations = patients * 0.1  # Genetic variations matter
total_decisions_needed = diseases * treatments_per_disease * patient_variations
# = 800,000,000,000 decisions needed

# Time for committee to process everything

years_to_process = total_decisions_needed / (committee_capacity * 365)
print(f"Years for FDA to evaluate everything: {years_to_process:,.0f}")
# Output: 1,369,863 years

# Market processing (parallel, decentralized)

![Eight billion people all thinking at the same time about medicine. Like a very large brain made of smaller brains, which sounds horrifying but is apparently efficient.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-market-processing-parallel-decentralized-bw-academic.jpg)

market_participants = 8_000_000_000
market_decisions_per_day = market_participants * 1  # One health decision per person
market_years = total_decisions_needed / (market_decisions_per_day * 365)
print(f"Years for decentralized system: {market_years:.2f}")
# Output: 0.27 years (100 days)
```

**The committee needs 1.3 million years. The decentralized system needs 100 days.**

![Time required to evaluate all potential treatment variations: Centralized Committee (1.3 million years) vs. Decentralized Market (100 days).](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-centralized-vs-decentralized-processing-time-bw-academic.jpg)

### Why 200 People Can't Replace 8 Billion

The FDA doesn't know:

- What disease **you** have (they haven't met you)
- How **your** body responds to treatments (genetics are unique)
- What risks **you're** willing to take (some prefer death to side effects, others the reverse)
- Whether **you'd** rather die trying or die waiting (only you can answer this)

But they decide for you anyway.

![One committee in Maryland trying to decide what medicine works for 8 billion different people. It's like having one person choose shoes for the entire planet.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-why-200-people-can-t-replace-8-billion-bw-academic.jpg)

### The Solution: Let 8 Billion Experts Make 8 Billion Decisions

#### Current system

```
330 Million Americans
        ↓
   200 FDA Bureaucrats (Bottleneck)
        ↓
    17-Year Delays
        ↓
    Millions Die
```

**Decentralized system:**

```
8 Billion Humans
    ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ ↓ (Parallel Processing)
Millions of Trials Simultaneously
        ↓
    Real-Time Results
        ↓
    Data Saves Everyone
```

This isn't ideology. It's information theory. You mathematically cannot centralize medical decisions for 8 billion unique people. The FDA could work 24/7 for a million years and still be behind.

The only solution is to let patients and doctors make their own decisions, then pool the data so everyone benefits from everyone's experience.

## Your Personal Death-Prevention Assistant: The FDAi

Everyone gets a superintelligent doctor that lives in their phone and doesn't judge them for Googling "is my poop normal?"

![Your watch tells the computer what's killing you. The computer tells you what might unkill you. We've had the watches for 15 years but kept the parts separate.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-your-personal-death-prevention-assistant-the-fdai-bw-academic.jpg)

The **FDAi** (Food and Drug Artificial intelligence) is like Siri, but instead of telling you the weather, it tells you how not to die.

**You**: "I have diabetes and my foot fell off."
**FDAi**: "Based on 50,000 similar cases, here's what worked:

- 60% success: Reattachment surgery + Drug A
- 30% success: Prosthetic foot + Drug B  
- 10% success: Hopping lessons + Prayer
- 0% success: Essential oils (but your remaining foot will smell lavender-fresh)"

It does this by connecting to all your data, from wearables, apps, and your medical records, and looking for patterns. It's automated root cause analysis for your own body, finding what's wrong while your doctor is still trying to remember your name. It's like having every doctor who ever lived in your pocket, except they actually agree on something.

## The Disease Eradication Act: Making It Legal to Not Die

<img src="../../assets/images/right_to_trial_act_image.jpg" alt="Disease Eradication Act" style="max-width: 600px; width: 100%;" />

This solution requires a law that says: "Dying people can try things that might help them not die."

The fact that we need a law for this tells you everything about our species.

**The Right to Trial Act** (working title: "The Stop Being Stupid About Medicine Act"):

**Section 1**: If you're dying, you can try experimental treatments.
**Section 2**: What happens is written down.
**Section 3**: Other dying people can read what is written.
**Section 4**: Repeat until nobody's dying.
**Section 5**: Seriously, how was this not already the law?

Congress will debate this for 17 years, the same time it takes to approve one drug.

## The Future: Where Death Becomes Embarrassing

### 2027: The Beginning of the End of Dying Slowly

FDA.gov becomes actually useful. Millions join trials from home. The first "Wikipedia disease" gets cured entirely through crowdsourced trials. The FDA claims credit.

![Medical research you can do in your pajamas. Take pill, report results, help science. Like jury duty but you might live longer.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-2027-the-beginning-of-the-end-of-dying-slowly-bw-academic.jpg)

### 2030: Big Pharma Pivots or Dies

Pharmaceutical companies realize they can't charge $10,000 for pills that cost $1 to make when everyone can see the data. Some adapt. Some become museums.

### 2035: The Great Revelation

We realize we could have done this all along. We had the internet since 1990. We had computers since 1950. We had writing since 3000 BC.

![Humans invented writing, then printing, then computers. Then used all three to make filling out forms take longer.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-2035-the-great-revelation-bw-academic.jpg)

We spent 5,000 years letting people die while we filled out forms.

History books will call us "The Paperwork Age" and children will laugh at our stupidity.

### 2050: Death Becomes Opt-In

Diseases are mostly solved. Death becomes a choice, like smoking or voting Republican. The FDA's job becomes preventing people from becoming immortal too quickly (traffic is bad enough).

![Before the FDA: death was optional if you could afford medicine. After the FDA: death is mandatory unless you fill out the right paperwork.](/assets/images/dfda/dfda-section-2050-death-becomes-opt-in-bw-academic.jpg)

The last FDA form is filled out. It's immediately lost. Nobody notices.
